blindSummary:
This state/province, an autonomous territory, is the unit where a structurally different legal system can apply to a visitor in conflict situations. Its administrative framework (a 2019 code) provides that justice in the autonomous region be dispensed “in consonance with the constitution, religious law, and traditional or tribal laws.” A parliamentary bill (July 2026) proposes a comprehensive religious justice code adding discretionary religious criminal offences — the category under which morality offences against same-sex conduct and gender expression are prosecuted in comparable systems. Nationally, the religious court system is expanding: the head of state signed a law in August 2024 creating three new religious-court districts and twelve circuit courts beyond the autonomous territory, a 2025 law aims at equitable access, and in January 2026 the national high court resolved to operationalise the religious high court.

The dossier's assessor caveat is explicit: no source establishes that the country's religious courts currently prosecute same-sex conduct or gender expression, and the 1977 decree that created them codified only personal law. The finding is structural — a jurisdiction with an active legislative process to create criminal religious law, in a region where a visitor's dispute may be adjudicated outside the national court system entirely — rather than a documented enforcement reality. No protective ordinance or civil-rights infrastructure is documented in the autonomous territory.
blindSourceSummaries: Full text of the autonomous territory's 2019 administrative code, from its official gazette: prescribes the structures and rules of governance of the autonomous region (the cached extract covers the introductory provisions; the justice-dispensation clause — 'in consonance with the constitution, religious law, traditional or tribal laws' — is cited in the dossier), while guaranteeing religious freedom.

The autonomous parliament's release (14 July 2026): a proposed bill for a comprehensive religious justice system code governing religious civil actions, religious commercial transactions, supplementary family relations under religious law, discretionary religious criminal offences, alternative dispute resolution and religious arbitration; the discretionary-offence category is the one under which morality offences against same-sex conduct and gender expression are prosecuted in comparable systems (cached page body largely site navigation).

An overseas religious-news report (November 2024): in August 2024 the head of state signed a law creating three new religious judicial districts and twelve circuit courts, spreading the religious court system beyond the autonomous territory into parts of the country where another faith is predominant, including the capital region; church leaders there mostly learned of it months later; the religious court system was originally established in 1977.

Full text of the 1977 decree on personal law for one religious community: creates religious district and circuit courts as courts of limited jurisdiction within the national judicial system under the highest court's supervision, applying only to adherents of that faith, and codifying personal law — personal status, marriage and divorce, matrimonial and family relations, succession and inheritance — not criminal offences.
